title: Hybrid Retrieval
text: Hybrid retrieval combines two complementary ranking signals for the same query: a sparse lexical score such as BM25 and a dense semantic score from vector embeddings. Each retriever produces its own ranked list, and a fusion step such as Reciprocal Rank Fusion merges the lists into a single ranking. Hybrid retrieval is used because exact keyword match and semantic similarity fail in different situations: BM25 finds exact identifiers that embeddings miss, while dense retrieval finds paraphrases that lexical matching misses.

title: BM25 Sparse Retrieval
text: BM25 is a bag-of-words ranking function that scores documents using term frequency, inverse document frequency, and document length normalization. Rare query terms receive a higher IDF weight. The k1 parameter controls how quickly term frequency saturates and b controls length normalization. BM25 is strong when a query contains exact tokens such as error codes, table names, or product identifiers, because the score depends on literal term overlap rather than vector similarity.

title: Reciprocal Rank Fusion
text: Reciprocal Rank Fusion, or RRF, merges several ranked lists into one ranking without needing score normalization. For every document, RRF sums contributions of 1 divided by (k + rank) from each list where the document appears, with rank starting at 1. A common constant is k = 60, which dampens the influence of very high ranks. RRF is popular because raw scores from BM25 and cosine similarity are on incompatible scales, while rank positions are directly comparable.

title: Dense Vector Retrieval
text: Dense vector retrieval encodes queries and documents into embedding vectors and ranks documents by cosine similarity. It handles paraphrases well: a query about late-paying customers can match a document about delinquent accounts even when no words overlap. Dense retrieval is weaker on rare exact identifiers, because an embedding may place an unseen code like JOB_7841 or AR_90_PLUS far from a query that names it literally.

title: Retrieval Evaluation Metrics
text: Retrieval quality is measured with labeled evaluation sets where each query has known relevant document ids. Recall at k measures the fraction of relevant documents retrieved in the top k. Mean Reciprocal Rank rewards putting the first relevant document high in the list. Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain discounts relevant documents found deeper in the ranking. Precision at k reports how much of the top k is relevant. Evaluating retrieval before generation isolates failures in the search layer from failures in the language model layer.

title: RRF Fusion Formula
text: The Reciprocal Rank Fusion score for a document is the sum over all ranked lists of 1 / (k + rank), where k is a smoothing constant and rank is the document position in each list starting at 1. A document ranked first in both BM25 and dense retrieval scores 2 / (k + 1), while a document ranked first in only one list scores 1 / (k + 1). With k = 60 the contribution of rank 1 is about 0.0164. The value of k is a convention, not a universal optimum, and teams tune it per collection.

title: Cross-Encoder Reranking
text: A cross-encoder reranker reads the query and a candidate document together in one transformer pass and outputs a relevance score for the pair. This is slower than bi-encoder retrieval because every candidate requires a full forward pass, so reranking is applied only to a shortlist, for example the top 10 documents from hybrid retrieval. Reranking can fix ordering mistakes that fusion leaves behind, but it cannot recover documents that the first stage never fetched.

title: When Hybrid Retrieval Helps
text: Hybrid retrieval helps most on mixed queries that contain both business language and technical identifiers. A query asking which job refreshes the invoice aging mart names an exact identifier that BM25 ranks first, while a query about chronic late payers paraphrases a glossary entry that dense retrieval ranks first. Pure dense or pure sparse systems miss one of these two query styles; fused hybrid retrieval handles both because each signal contributes its own ranked list.

title: Chunking Strategy
text: Chunking splits source documents into passages before indexing. Chunk size commonly ranges from 300 to 800 tokens, and an overlap of 50 to 100 tokens preserves context across chunk boundaries. Each chunk is embedded once for the dense index and tokenized once for the BM25 index. Too-large chunks dilute the signal for retrieval scoring, while too-small chunks lose the surrounding context needed to answer a question.

title: Evaluation Set Design
text: A retrieval evaluation set pairs each query with the document ids that a correct system should return. Labels can be binary relevant or not relevant, or graded. The set must be fixed and version controlled so that metric changes between runs reflect pipeline changes rather than label changes. For a small local suite, ten to twenty labeled queries over a corpus of tens of documents is enough to compare BM25, dense, and hybrid strategies.

title: Mean Reciprocal Rank
text: Mean Reciprocal Rank, or MRR, is the average over queries of the reciprocal of the rank of the first relevant document. A document at rank 1 contributes 1.0, rank 2 contributes 0.5, and rank 10 contributes 0.1. MRR only inspects the first relevant hit, so it suits question answering where the user needs one good document. It ignores additional relevant documents deeper in the list, which recall at k captures instead.

title: Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain
text: Discounted Cumulative Gain sums relevance values divided by a logarithmic rank discount, so relevant documents near the top contribute more. Normalized DCG divides by the ideal DCG of the same query, which places all relevant documents at the top, keeping the score between 0 and 1. Unlike MRR, nDCG rewards every relevant document in the list, not just the first one, which makes it informative for multi-document answers.

title: Sparse Versus Dense Failure Modes
text: Sparse lexical retrieval fails on vocabulary mismatch: the document says delinquent accounts while the query says customers who do not pay. Dense retrieval fails on rare identifiers and out-of-vocabulary tokens such as internal job ids or schema field names, because such tokens may barely influence the embedding. Hybrid retrieval with rank fusion exists precisely because these failure modes are complementary, and evaluating both strategies separately makes the difference visible in the metrics.

title: Embedding Models for CPU Retrieval
text: Small sentence embedding models such as all-MiniLM-L6-v2 produce 384-dimensional vectors and run comfortably on CPU, encoding a small corpus in seconds. Larger models improve quality on hard semantic tasks but require more memory and latency. The model name should stay configurable so the same evaluation harness can compare encoders without code changes. Embeddings are L2 normalized so cosine similarity reduces to a dot product.

title: Retrieval Before Generation
text: In a retrieval-augmented generation system the language model can only use documents the retriever fetched, so retrieval failures become unfixable answer failures. Measuring recall at k on a labeled set tells you whether the right evidence was available at all, before spending effort on prompt tuning or model selection. This is why retrieval evaluation is the first checkpoint in any RAG pipeline review.

title: Invoice Aging Mart Schema
text: The finance warehouse publishes a table named fact_invoice_aging. The primary customer key is cust_id and the invoice key is invoice_id. The overdue bucket for invoices more than 90 days past due is AR_90_PLUS. The collections_priority_code field identifies which overdue accounts should be worked first. Analysts frequently search for the exact identifiers fact_invoice_aging, cust_id, invoice_id, AR_90_PLUS, and collections_priority_code.

title: Invoice Aging Mart Refresh Job
text: The mart.finance.invoice_aging_daily table is refreshed every morning by job_7841. The refresh job writes snapshot_date, region_code, overdue_bucket, and invoice_amount columns. Downstream dashboards such as dashboard_ar_watchlist read from this mart. If the mart is stale, operators first check whether job_7841 completed successfully before inspecting landing paths and transformation logs.

title: Collections Glossary
text: Collections teams use the phrase chronic late payers for customers who repeatedly miss due dates and keep balances unpaid for long periods. Business users describe AR_90_PLUS as the bucket for customers who are very late on payments. Analysts looking for accounts with old unpaid balances, delinquent invoices, or severe delinquency usually phrase these questions in business language rather than with warehouse field names.

title: Data Quality Checks for Aging Data
text: The finance quality checklist verifies that overdue_bucket totals reconcile with the aging report and that region_code counts match the source extract. When AR_90_PLUS totals drift, analysts inspect snapshot_date freshness, duplicate invoice_id values, and delayed refresh jobs. The checklist combines exact technical terms with operational language about stale reports and aging snapshots.

title: Refund Policy Overview
text: Store credits can be requested within thirty days of purchase when an amount is incorrect. Refund operations belong to post-purchase support workflows and are unrelated to receivables monitoring, invoice aging, or collections processes.

title: Shipping Updates and Alerts
text: Shipping alerts are generated from logistics systems and do not depend on finance pipelines. Delivery exceptions and route changes are handled by the operations team and are unrelated to receivables buckets or collector workflows.

title: FAISS Vector Index
text: FAISS is a library for fast nearest-neighbor search over embedding vectors. For a small corpus a brute-force inner product search is exact and fast enough, which makes FAISS a common local choice for dense retrieval prototypes. The index stores one vector per chunk and returns the nearest neighbors for a query embedding, which the retriever converts into a ranked document list.
